subject: Agriculture
title: True Cost Accounting
description: A short lesson to help you apply True Cost Accounting.

hook.text: A $1 hamburger costs $1 at the register. But society pays $6 more in health, environmental, and social costs.

buildup.text: True cost accounting quantifies hidden costs: water pollution, soil erosion, emissions, and diet-related disease.

discovery.text: The Rockefeller Foundation found the US food system's hidden costs total $3.2 trillion per year—double its revenues.

twist.text: If these costs were included in prices, organic and sustainable food would often be cheaper than conventional.

climax.text: True cost pricing could transform food choices overnight—but no government has implemented it at scale.

punchline.text: Cheap food is an illusion. Someone pays. Just not at the checkout.

quiz.question: What did the Rockefeller Foundation estimate as the US food system's annual hidden costs?

details.summary: True cost accounting measures the full environmental, social, and health costs of food production that are not reflected in market prices. This topic covers hidden costs of conventional agriculture—pollution, health impacts, and biodiversity loss—and how accounting for them changes the value.
details.whyItMatters: Conventional food prices are kept artificially low because environmental damage, health costs, and resource depletion are externalized. True cost accounting reveals that organic and sustainable food may actually be cheaper when all costs are.
takeaways: Conventional agriculture externalizes costs like water pollution and health impacts
True cost accounting adds these hidden costs to reveal the real price of cheap food
Studies show organic food often costs less when environmental externalities are included

faq.question: What hidden costs does conventional agriculture create?
faq.answer: Major externalities include water pollution from fertilizer runoff, healthcare costs from pesticide exposure, antibiotic resistance from livestock operations, soil degradation that reduces future productivity, and biodiversity loss from habitat destruction.

faq.question: How does true cost accounting change the organic vs. conventional debate?
faq.answer: When environmental cleanup, health costs, and resource depletion are factored in, the price gap between organic and conventional food narrows dramatically or reverses. A 2018 study found conventional food would cost twice as much if externalities were included in the price.
